reference_title: Ground Modification Methods Reference Manual – Volume II

sections.title: Description
sections.body: Geosynthetic reinforcement encompasses the use of geosynthetic materials (primarily geogrids and woven geotextiles) as horizontal tensile reinforcement within soil fills to create reinforced soil structures including mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) walls, reinforced soil slopes (RSS), and reinforced embankments. The geosynthetic provides tensile resistance to maintain internal stability of the reinforced mass, reducing lateral earth pressure on facing elements and improving global stability. Geosynthetics for reinforcement are characterized by tensile strength (short-term and long-term), stiffness (tensile modulus), and interaction with soil (pullout and direct shear resistance). The two primary product types are geogrids (open grid structure, primarily interlocked with aggregate) and woven geotextiles (continuous fabric providing both reinforcement and separation functions). GEC-11 (FHWA-NHI-10-024) is the primary design reference for MSE walls and reinforced soil slopes; GEC-13 Chapter 11 provides a summary within the broader ground modification context, including geosynthetic-reinforced embankments over soft soils and column-supported embankments.
key_points: Geogrids and woven geotextiles placed as horizontal layers in fill to provide tensile reinforcement
Applications: MSE walls, reinforced soil slopes (RSS), reinforced embankments over soft ground
Tensile resistance limits lateral earth pressure and improves global stability
Geogrids: open structure interlocking with aggregate; woven geotextiles: fabric with reinforcement + separation
Key properties: tensile strength (LTDS), stiffness (modulus), pullout resistance, direct shear resistance
Primary MSE/RSS design reference: FHWA GEC-11 (FHWA-NHI-10-024)

sections.applicability: MSE walls, reinforced soil slopes, and reinforced embankments over soft or unstable foundation soils.

sections.title: Geosynthetic Types and Properties
sections.body: Geogrids are polymeric grid structures with ribs and junction nodes that provide high interface friction and passive resistance with surrounding soil. They are manufactured from polyester (PET), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), or polypropylene (PP) by extrusion-stretching (uniaxial or biaxial) or welding. Woven geotextiles are manufactured from PET or PP yarns woven into a fabric; they provide reinforcement in both primary and secondary directions and also perform filtration functions. Long-term design strength (LTDS) is the key geosynthetic reinforcement design property; LTDS = T_ult / (RF_ID × RF_CR × RF_CBD × FS), where T_ult is the ultimate tensile strength and the RF terms are reduction factors for installation damage (RF_ID), creep (RF_CR), chemical/biological degradation (RF_CBD), and an overall factor of safety (FS). For PET geogrids, RF_CR ≈ 1.6–2.5; for HDPE, RF_CR ≈ 2.5–5.0 (higher creep susceptibility). Durability requirements for geosynthetics in transportation applications are specified in AASHTO M288 and GEC-11 Table 3-3.
key_points: Geogrids: polymeric grid (PET, HDPE, or PP), extruded-stretched or welded; high soil-geosynthetic interaction
Woven geotextiles: PET or PP fabric; provides reinforcement + filtration/separation
Long-term design strength LTDS = T_ult / (RF_ID × RF_CR × RF_CBD × FS)
Creep reduction factors: RF_CR ≈ 1.6–2.5 (PET), 2.5–5.0 (HDPE)
Durability limits per AASHTO M288 and GEC-11 Table 3-3
Geosynthetic selection should include pullout resistance testing with project-specific backfill
equations: Eq 11-1: Long-term design strength LTDS = T_ult / (RF_ID × RF_CR × RF_CBD × FS)
Eq 11-2: Pullout capacity per unit width F_p = C_i × φ × σ_v × L_e × α (interaction coefficient method)

sections.title: Reinforced Embankments Over Soft Soils
sections.body: Geosynthetic reinforcement in embankments over soft soils serves to increase bearing capacity and global stability, reduce lateral spreading of fill, and provide differential settlement mitigation. Failure modes addressed by embankment reinforcement include: (1) bearing capacity failure (foundation shear failure), where the geosynthetic increases the allowable bearing pressure by providing a confining tension; (2) rotational failure through the embankment and soft foundation, where the geosynthetic provides a restoring moment; and (3) lateral spreading of the embankment fill (squeezing), where tensile resistance in the geosynthetic limits horizontal deformation. Design methods per FHWA NHI course and BS 8006 include limit equilibrium analysis of slip circles through the embankment base, with the geosynthetic force applied as a concentrated force at the slip circle exit point. Required tensile strength T_req is determined from the stability analysis deficit, and the geosynthetic must provide this strength within allowable strain limits (typically 5–10% strain). Embankment staging and consolidation monitoring are often combined with geosynthetic reinforcement to further improve stability and reduce total settlement.
key_points: Geosynthetic reinforcement addresses bearing capacity failure, rotational failure, and lateral spreading
Design: limit equilibrium with geosynthetic force at slip circle exit; T_req from stability deficit
Allowable strain typically 5–10% for embankment applications
Geosynthetic provides both tensile resistance and drainage function (woven geotextile) at embankment base
Combined with embankment staging and consolidation monitoring for improved performance
High-strength geosynthetics (200–1,000 kN/m) required for embankments over very soft soils
equations: Eq 11-3: Required geosynthetic tensile force T_req = (FS_req - FS_unreinforced) × W_embankment × sin(α) / n_layers
Eq 11-4: Factor of safety FS = (sum of resisting moments + T × moment_arm) / (sum of driving moments)
figures: Figure 11-2: Limit equilibrium model for geosynthetic-reinforced embankment over soft ground showing failure circle, geosynthetic force, and moment arms
sections.applicability: Embankments over soft cohesive foundation soils where bearing capacity or global stability is insufficient without reinforcement.

sections.title: MSE Walls and Reinforced Soil Slopes
sections.body: Mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) walls use closely spaced horizontal geosynthetic (or metallic) reinforcement layers within compacted granular backfill to create a composite gravity wall system. Internal design per AASHTO LRFD checks: reinforcement tensile rupture, reinforcement pullout, and connection strength between reinforcement and facing. External design checks global stability, sliding, overturning, and bearing capacity of the reinforced mass. Reinforced soil slopes (RSS) use geosynthetic reinforcement at wider spacing within compacted fill to construct slopes steeper than the unreinforced friction angle (typically 70–85° from horizontal for well-reinforced slopes). RSS design uses limit equilibrium with internal reinforcement forces. Both MSE walls and RSS are designed per FHWA GEC-11 (FHWA-NHI-10-024), which provides the detailed LRFD design procedure, reinforcement spacing requirements, facing design, and construction specifications. GEC-13 Chapter 11 does not duplicate GEC-11 design procedures but provides context for their place within the broader ground modification toolkit.
key_points: MSE walls: closely spaced geosynthetic reinforcement + compacted granular backfill + facing = composite gravity wall
Internal design: tensile rupture, pullout, connection strength (per AASHTO LRFD and GEC-11)
External design: global stability, sliding, overturning, bearing capacity of reinforced mass
Reinforced soil slopes (RSS): wider spacing, steeper than unreinforced friction angle (70–85°)
Full MSE wall and RSS design procedures in GEC-11 (FHWA-NHI-10-024); GEC-13 provides overview only
Select structural fill (PI < 6, D15 < 0.9 mm, pH 5–10) required for geosynthetic reinforcement backfill
sections.applicability: MSE walls and reinforced soil slopes; refer to GEC-11 for full design procedures.

sections.title: Geosynthetic Reinforcement in Column-Supported Embankments
sections.body: In column-supported embankments (CSE), geosynthetic reinforcement within the load transfer platform (LTP) is an integral component that enables load transfer from the embankment to the column heads by tensile membrane action. The geosynthetic is placed at the base of the granular LTP, at mid-height, or in multiple layers, and is subjected to vertical load from the embankment fill transmitted through the arching mechanism in the granular LTP. Design methods for geosynthetic in CSE (BS 8006, EBGEO) determine the required tensile strength from the load not intercepted by soil arching and the geometry of the unsupported span between column heads. Typical required tensile strengths in CSE applications range from 100–400 kN/m. The geosynthetic must also provide sufficient stiffness to limit deflection between column heads (differential settlement at the LTP base), which is typically limited to 1–2% of the clear span. Refer to GEC-13 Chapter 6 for CSE system design and this chapter for geosynthetic property requirements.
key_points: Geosynthetic in CSE: placed at base or mid-height of granular LTP; provides tensile membrane load transfer
Required tensile strength determined from load not intercepted by arching: 100–400 kN/m typical
Must limit differential deflection between column heads to typically 1–2% of clear span
Design per BS 8006 or EBGEO methods (detailed in GEC-13 Chapter 6)
Geosynthetic stiffness (tensile modulus at design strain) as important as peak strength for deflection control
Multi-layer geosynthetics may be used for larger column spacings or higher embankment loads
equations: Eq 11-5: Geosynthetic tension in CSE per unit width T = H_col / (8 × ε_s) × (q_col × s_net) from membrane analogy
where H_col = load on geosynthetic between columns, s_net = clear span, ε_s = design strain
sections.applicability: Geosynthetic reinforcement design within LTP of column-supported embankments.

sections.title: Construction and Quality Assurance
sections.body: Geosynthetic reinforcement installation requires careful attention to: orientation (primary strength direction perpendicular to wall or in direction of maximum tension); seam and overlap requirements (typically 0.6–1.5 m overlap for embankment applications; mechanical connections for MSE walls); protection from installation damage (damage reduction factor RF_ID determined by backfill gradation); and compaction procedures (avoid heavy compaction equipment directly on geosynthetic until covered by at least 150 mm of fill). Geosynthetic rolls must be stored and handled to avoid UV degradation (cover with opaque material; limit UV exposure to <30 days for PP products). Quality assurance includes: identity testing of delivered materials (ASTM D4595 or D6637 tensile testing, ASTM D4632 grab strength); visual inspection for damage; and documentation of seam/overlap lengths. Survivability testing of geosynthetic samples extracted from beneath fill after compaction verifies that installation damage is within the RF_ID assumed in design.
key_points: Orientation: primary strength direction perpendicular to wall or in direction of maximum tension
Overlaps: 0.6–1.5 m for embankments; mechanical connections for MSE wall facing
Avoid heavy compaction equipment on geosynthetic until covered by minimum 150 mm of fill
UV protection required for PP geosynthetics; limit UV exposure to <30 days
QA: identity testing (ASTM D4595/D6637 tensile, D4632 grab strength), visual inspection, seam documentation
Survivability testing: extract samples from beneath fill after compaction to verify RF_ID
sections.applicability: Installation and quality assurance for geosynthetic reinforcement in walls, slopes, embankments, and CSE.

sections.title: References
sections.body: Primary references for geosynthetic reinforcement design include: FHWA GEC-11 (FHWA-NHI-10-024, Elias et al. 2009) for MSE walls and RSS; FHWA-HI-95-038 (Holtz et al. 1995) for geosynthetics for reinforcement and drainage; AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications Sections 11.10 (MSE walls) and 3.11 (earth pressures); BS 8006:2010 for reinforced fills including CSE and embankments; EBGEO (2010) German recommendations for geosynthetic-reinforced embankments; and Koerner (2012) Designing with Geosynthetics textbook. Geosynthetic property test standards include ASTM D4595, D6637 (tensile), D4632 (grab), D4533 (trapezoid tear), and ASTM D6770 (pullout). Durability standards are AASHTO M288 and GRI GC-8/GG-4/GT-12.
key_points: MSE walls and RSS: FHWA GEC-11 (FHWA-NHI-10-024)
General geosynthetic reinforcement: FHWA-HI-95-038 (Holtz et al. 1995)
CSE geosynthetic design: BS 8006:2010 and EBGEO (2010)
AASHTO M288 for durability requirements; GRI standards for specific applications
ASTM D4595 and D6637 for tensile properties; D4632 for grab strength; D6770 for pullout
Koerner (2012) Designing with Geosynthetics: standard textbook reference
sections.applicability: Bibliography and key design references for geosynthetic reinforcement applications.
